topic: Databricks Certified Machine Learning Associate exam preparation - using the Databricks Machine Learning platform (AutoML, Feature Store, Unity Catalog, MLflow, and clusters), performing data processing and machine-learning workflows, developing and tuning models, and deploying machine-learning models on Databricks
exam_format: Approximately 45 scored questions (some published sources cite up to 48, plus a small number of unscored research items) in a 90-minute online, remotely proctored exam. Question types are multiple choice (one correct answer) and multiple response (two or more correct answers). The passing score is commonly cited around 70 percent, though Databricks scores on overall performance and may adjust the exact threshold - present the question count, time limit, and passing score as APPROXIMATE and tell candidates to confirm the current figures on Databricks' official Machine Learning Associate exam guide before scheduling. The registration fee is approximately USD 200 plus any local tax. The certification is valid for two years, after which recertification on the current exam is required. Databricks periodically updates the exam guide, so tell candidates to verify the current domains and weights on the official page. This is a closed-book exam - no notes, documentation, or external tools are permitted.
question_types: multiple choice (single answer, exactly 4 options) and multiple response clearly marked 'Choose TWO/THREE'; practical, scenario-based items asking which Databricks feature, workflow step, modeling choice, or deployment approach is correct for a described machine-learning situation - NOT rote definitions
audience: Data scientists, machine-learning engineers, data engineers with an ML focus, and early-career AI/ML practitioners who build and deploy machine-learning workflows on Databricks. Databricks recommends roughly six months of hands-on experience with the platform (Python, Spark ML, Feature Store, and MLflow); no formal prerequisite is required. A strong platform-specific complement to the vendor-neutral and other-vendor ML courses in this catalog (AWS MLA-C01, Google Cloud Professional ML Engineer) and a foundation for the Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate and Machine Learning Professional paths.
author: Aseem Mankotia

domains.name: Databricks Machine Learning
domains.notes: The heaviest domain - the Databricks ML platform itself: Databricks Runtime for Machine Learning and ML clusters; AutoML for baseline model generation and the generated notebooks; the Feature Store / Feature Engineering in Unity Catalog for creating, storing, and serving features; Unity Catalog for governing data, features, and models; MLflow Tracking (runs, parameters, metrics, artifacts) and the MLflow Model Registry / models in Unity Catalog; and using notebooks, jobs, and Repos for ML work. Choosing the correct Databricks capability or MLflow component for a described ML task.

domains.name: ML Workflows
domains.notes: The end-to-end machine-learning workflow on Databricks: exploratory data analysis and data cleaning; feature engineering and transformations (handling missing values, encoding categoricals, scaling); train/validation/test splitting and avoiding data leakage; and preparing data at scale with Spark and pandas API on Spark. Choosing the correct data-processing or workflow step for a described dataset and modeling goal.

domains.name: Model Development
domains.notes: Building, tuning, and evaluating models: training classical models (for example scikit-learn and Spark ML pipelines), single-node vs distributed training considerations; hyperparameter tuning with Hyperopt (including SparkTrials) and grid/random search; cross-validation and evaluation metrics for classification and regression; tracking experiments and comparing runs in MLflow; and model selection. Choosing the correct training approach, tuning strategy, or evaluation metric for a described modeling problem.

domains.name: Model Deployment
domains.notes: Getting models into production: batch and streaming inference on Databricks; real-time serving with Model Serving endpoints; loading models from the MLflow Model Registry / Unity Catalog; applying models as Spark UDFs for scaled batch scoring; and awareness of deployment patterns and when each fits. Choosing the correct deployment or inference approach for a described latency and scale requirement.

extra_guidance: Databricks Certified Machine Learning Associate is Databricks' associate-level, platform-specific ML credential and a strong complement to the vendor-neutral and other-vendor ML courses in this catalog (AWS MLA-C01, Google Cloud Professional ML Engineer), plus a foundation for the Databricks Certified Generative AI Engineer Associate (already in this catalog) and the Machine Learning Professional path. The exam is PRACTICAL and PLATFORM-CENTRIC: the real skill it tests is 'given this ML scenario on Databricks, which platform feature, workflow step, modeling choice, or deployment approach is correct,' NOT memorizing ML theory. The four domain names and weights above are Databricks' official Machine Learning Associate exam-guide weightings (Databricks Machine Learning 38%, ML Workflows 19%, Model Development 31%, Model Deployment 12%) - use them verbatim, and note Databricks updates the guide periodically so learners should verify on the official Databricks exam page. This is a READ-AND-UNDERSTAND, notebook-centric course - show and explain real Databricks and MLflow usage (AutoML runs, Feature Store / feature engineering in Unity Catalog, MLflow Tracking and the Model Registry / models in Unity Catalog, Hyperopt tuning, Model Serving) and the Python/Spark ML code as it appears; make clear that the free Databricks Community Edition or a trial workspace is enough to follow along and no paid workspace is required. Use EXACT current Databricks terminology and call out the commonly confused pairs the exam loves: AutoML vs manual model building; Feature Store/feature engineering in Unity Catalog vs ad-hoc features; MLflow Tracking vs the Model Registry / models in Unity Catalog; Hyperopt SparkTrials (parallel single-node) vs distributed Spark ML training; single-node scikit-learn vs distributed Spark ML; batch vs streaming vs real-time Model Serving; and pandas API on Spark vs single-node pandas. Flag classic traps: data leakage from fitting transformers before the train/test split; when to use a Spark UDF to scale batch inference; choosing Model Serving for low-latency real-time vs batch scoring for throughput; and Unity Catalog governance of features and models. Anchor everything to real, current Databricks behavior and published docs (the Databricks ML documentation, MLflow, Unity Catalog, AutoML, and Model Serving guides); do NOT invent feature names, limits, or APIs, and prefer current names (models in Unity Catalog / Feature Engineering in Unity Catalog) while noting older names where the exam may still use them. NEVER promise a pass or use the word 'guarantee' in ANY form (Udemy compliance) - use 'exam-focused preparation' framing throughout, including the learning objectives and who-this-is-for. Present the exam fee as approximate (~USD 200 plus tax) and note the two-year validity and closed-book, online-proctored format. The final chapter must be a full exam simulation with a 90-minute, ~45-question time-management strategy. Scan the practice bank for stray other-vendor terms (AWS SageMaker, Azure ML, Google Vertex AI, Snowflake) before upload per the pipeline compliance rules - keep all platform references Databricks-specific.
